# Possession labelling for BAR-ATH — technical document

*More than a Hack 2027, Phase 1. Team: [team name, members]. Repository: [public URL].*
*Submission: `candidate_v20.csv` (199,319 rows), MD5 `d909212952998c76568b09c17b76b5d5`, regenerated by
`python src/make_submission.py` (section 10).*

## 1. Summary

Every frame is labelled by a two-part probabilistic model and a duration-aware decoder:

1. **Dead ball (D vs alive)** comes from four pieces of evidence whose weights and models all come from open data: a small rule
   model on player tempo and the ball's position and movement, a dead-ball classifier trained on three open providers, a
   sequence model on the same tracking features, with every input scaled by the half's own level, and whether the aligned
   broadcast recording shows the pitch (replays and close-ups are almost always dead time) (section 3.7).
2. **Team in possession (H vs A)** comes from a gradient-boosted classifier on team-level tracking features. It is
   trained only on open data: the 7 IDSSE / DFL Bundesliga matches and the 3 Metrica Sports sample games. Their clean
   tracking is first degraded by a simulator so that it looks like Metrica's automatic single-camera tracking: ball
   dropouts, smooth position noise, aerial-ball parallax and fragmented player tracks. Its probability is averaged in
   equal parts with that of a bidirectional GRU trained by a team member on open DFL and PFF data (section 3.3).
   Half of the final team probability comes from a **short-possession specialist**: a ball-centred tracking
   model trained on open PFF data and fine-tuned on the open DFL and Metrica games, whose labels follow the
   challenge's controlled-possession definition (section 3.6).
3. **A Viterbi decoder per half** combines both, with switch penalties, minimum durations and a soft minimum
   possession length. That length prior is what keeps the number of possessions realistic, which the ranking metric
   (spellF1) rewards.

Up to v19 a short-possession verifier took a second look at the decoder's short decisions (section 3.5). v20 does not use it.

The provided match was never used to choose between model versions from round 6 onwards. Model choices were made on
held-out external matches (section 6). On those, with dead-ball evidence built as on BAR-ATH, the submitted model reaches
spellF1 0.81–0.87 on the two full-pitch sets, 0.82–0.89 with the true dead ball, and 0.79 on SoccerTrack v2, which no model saw
(section 7).

## 2. Assets used and dropped

| Asset | Use |
|---|---|
| Tactical ATD (players, ball) | Main input. Own parser; `video_frame = frame_id - 1`; speed channel is m/s. |
| Tactical homography | Read by the feature builder (camera centre), but not used by the submitted model's evidence (the ATD is already in pitch coordinates). |
| Broadcast recording: ATD + homography | Aligned to the tactical timeline by a constant lag per half, found by matching ball positions: tactical = broadcast + 4,014 frames (1st half), + 26,920 (2nd half); the lag is constant to ±1–2 frames in every 2-minute block. Used for (a) dead-ball cues: no valid homography means a replay, close-up or crowd shot; (b) filling gaps in the tactical ball track where the broadcast shows live play that agrees with the tactical tracking. |
| Smart Tagging | Evaluated as team and restart evidence; its phase team agreed less with the reference than our own model, so it is not used. |
| Tactical video (images) | Not used in the submission. Ball detection on the wide tactical view (pretrained WASB, a YOLO fine-tuned on tracking pseudo-labels) did not reach a useful quality, and a perfect ball track is worth < +0.02 in simulation. |
| Tactical video audio | A referee-whistle detector was built (template from the kick-off whistles) but is **not** used in the submission: its only support was the 5-minute public window. |
| Broadcast audio / video | Investigated (commentary speech recognition, camera framing); neither helped on external validation, so neither is used. |
| Open data | IDSSE / DFL (Bassek et al. 2025, CC BY 4.0) and Metrica Sports sample data: training. PFF FC / Gradient Sports FIFA World Cup 2022 tracking (provider's access form): training of the bidirectional GRU and the specialist, independent test of the dead-ball evidence. SkillCorner open data (MIT): evaluation of the team side, training of the dead-ball models. SoccerTrack v2: independent test only. |

## 3. Method

### 3.1 Features of the provided match

Per frame: positions of all tracked players with their team (no identities), the ball where seen (the tactical ATD
ball, gaps filled from the aligned broadcast ball), nearest-player distances per team, players within fixed radii,
ball speed and stillness, ball beyond a line, time since the ball was last seen, broadcast-view validity and live
agreement. All team features are computed for both teams symmetrically, so the classifier sees "own side vs other
side" and is trained with a side swap.

### 3.2 Dead-ball evidence

The rule model is a weighted sum of these terms per frame, in alive log-odds:

- mean player speed over ±1 s and ±3 s, clipped, looked up 2 s ahead (players react to the referee late);
- ball beyond a line;
- ball unseen for more than 0.5 s;
- ball still (moved < 1 m over ±0.5 s);
- ball moving faster than 3 m/s inside the pitch.

The two view terms are broadcast without a valid homography (replay, close-up, crowd shot) and valid with at least four players
visible. Every threshold and weight comes from the open sets (section 3.7): `models/dead_rules_open_v1.json` is re-derived by
`src/dead_rules_fit.py`, and v20's `models/dead_rules_open_v2.json` keeps its thresholds with the weights refitted on `sim.V6` by
`src/dead_v6_fit.py`.

Frames between the end of the first half's grading window and the second kick-off are forced dead. The
rules up to v18 had the same form with hand-set constants, written on day one while checking them against the public window (see
section 6); v19 and v20 do not use them. From v16 to v17 a learned model timed
the boundaries of the rules' dead stretches (section 3.7).

### 3.3 Team-in-possession model

- **Labels.**
  - DFL: the per-frame BallPossession flag of the open data.
  - Metrica: built from the frame-synchronised events, read as *controlled* possession. The team is that of the last
    controlling event (set piece, pass, carry, recovery, shot, ball lost). Challenges, ball-out and fouls received do
    not change possession. A spell that follows the other team's spell counts as a change only if the new team shows
    control inside it: a completed pass or shot, or the ball kept for at least 1 s. Otherwise it is merged back into
    the previous team's possession. This mirrors the challenge definition: a touch without control, a deflection, or
    an aerial duel without subsequent control is not a change.
- **Simulated automatic tracking.**
  - Clean open tracking is degraded with `sim.V3`. The ball goes missing in long runs, more while the ball is dead
    and around stoppages, at rates calibrated to aggregate statistics of the provided tracking (no labels involved).
  - Position noise is low-passed: players 0.15 m, ball 0.35 m.
  - Aerial balls are projected to the ground through a high side camera, and player tracks are fragmented.
  - An adversarial-validation check against the provided tracking caught and removed an earlier version whose
    per-frame noise doubled all speeds.
  - v20's dead-ball models use `sim.V6`, which changes only the ball around stops and restarts (section 3.7); the team models stay on `sim.V3`.
- **Features.**
  - Nearest-player geometry, players within radii and a pressure-aware control score per team.
  - Own-half occupancy, set-piece formation, team shape and team movement.
  - Ball-free short-horizon team interactions: change of each team's spread (a team that wins the ball spreads out),
    speed of the last defensive line, reversal of the team centroid's direction, pressing velocity towards the
    nearest opponent, and supporting runs.
- **Model.**
  - LightGBM binary classifier: 400 rounds, learning rate 0.05, 63 leaves, min 200 samples per leaf, feature fraction
    0.8, bagging 0.7, L2 1.0. Deterministic mode, fixed seed, 8 threads; every 2nd frame is used for training.
  - Training data: 7 DFL matches (weight 1 each) and the 3 Metrica games, each in 3 degradations (weight 2 per game).
- **Blend with a sequence model.** The classifier's probability is averaged in equal parts with that of a
  bidirectional GRU (`models/bigru_dfl_pff_v1`: 64 units, dropout 0.15, 11 epochs, three seeds averaged) trained by a
  team member on the open DFL matches (their own possession flag) and on PFF World Cup 2022 tracking, with the same
  kind of degraded team-level inputs. The GRU alone is weaker than the classifier on DFL and Metrica, but the blend is
  better than either on most external contexts. The weight 0.5 was chosen from a grid fixed in advance (0.25 / 0.5 /
  0.75) by the worst-case regret over the external contexts (section 6).
- **Smoothing.** The blended probability's logits are averaged over ±25 frames (±1 s).

### 3.4 Decoding

Per half, a Viterbi decoder over {H, A, D} uses the emission scores S[H] = a/2 + log p, S[A] = a/2 + log(1 − p) and
S[D] = −a/2, where p is the smoothed probability that home has the ball. Log-probabilities are ≤ 0, so a confident
team call gives no bonus to "alive" over "dead". The decoder also uses:

- a switch penalty of 12 between H and A, and 30 between alive and dead;
- minimum durations of 8 frames for a possession and 50 frames for a dead-ball stretch;
- a soft minimum possession length: ending a possession after d < 175 frames costs an extra 48 · (1 − d/175).

The soft length prior was the largest single decoder gain. It discourages one-second flickers without forbidding
genuinely short possessions.

### 3.5 Short-possession verifier

v20 does not use the verifier: on v19's evidence it changed the primary contexts by +0.0002, and it has not been retrained on v20's base. It is described
because v13 to v19 use it. Possessions shorter than 4 s are 18–33% of the true possessions in the external sets but carry 36–47% of the lost
spellF1 credit. The team probability does point to the right team on most frames of 71–84% of them, but brief
wrong-team flips (≥ 0.5 s) inside long possessions are just as frequent (1.0–1.6 per alive minute against 0.8–1.7 true
short possessions), so the length prior has to suppress short changes; loosening it loses on DFL and Metrica. The
verifier therefore re-examines two kinds of candidates taken from the decoded output itself:

- *insert*: runs of ≥ 12 frames inside a decoded possession where the smoothed probability favours the other team;
- *delete*: decoded possessions shorter than 4 s.

Over the candidate interval only, it computes: ball visibility, speed and in-flight share; which team's players are
nearest to the ball and how close they get; touches detected by each team; distinct players of the candidate team
holding the ball and the longest hold; contested share; depth towards the candidate team's attack and distance to the
touchline; the change of each team's centroid speed (transition reaction); the time since the last decoded restart;
the lengths of the enclosing or neighbouring decoded possessions; the blended team probability's margin (smoothed and
raw); and the margin of the BiGRU alone (its three checkpoints averaged). Two LightGBM classifiers, one per candidate
type (`models/short_verifier_{ins,del}_g_blend50.txt`), are trained on the blend's candidates in the external sets
(DFL with the tracking-derived controlled labels, Metrica with the event-derived controlled labels, SkillCorner
phases). On DFL, whose matches all trained the shipped BiGRU, the BiGRU probabilities come from leave-one-match-out
copies of it (same recipe, retrained without that match), so that the classifiers learn from margins of a network
that never saw the match, as on BAR-ATH. A candidate is positive when at least half of its frames belong to the
candidate team and a true possession of that team overlaps it with IoU ≥ 0.3.

An insertion needs p ≥ 0.65 and must leave both parts of the enclosing possession at least the decoder's minimum
length. A deletion needs p < 0.35 and hands the frames to the other team only when that team holds a neighbouring
possession, never between two stoppages. In v15 the candidates and margins come from the base of section 3.6, the
specialist adds its own insert candidates and eight features, and the DFL and SkillCorner rows are labelled in the
controlled-possession reading (`models/short_verifier_{ins,del}_c1m25s.txt`).

### 3.6 Short-possession specialist (C1)

The external label conventions disagree mostly on short possessions: per match, Metrica's event-derived controlled
possessions have 12 short (< 4 s) in-play possessions between two possessions of the other team, DFL's event-derived
controlled reading 13, SkillCorner's phases 26 and its player possessions 37, PFF's own possessions 54 and DFL's raw
possession flag 135. The challenge defines possession as controlled possession (a touch, a deflection or an aerial duel
without subsequent control does not change it), which the Metrica and DFL event readings implement: a spell that
directly follows the other team's spell counts only if the new team shows control inside it (a completed pass, a shot,
or any of its on-ball events at least 0.5 s after the spell starts). The same reading applied to PFF's human-labelled
events gives 217 possessions per match, 21% short and 10 in play; applied to SkillCorner's dynamic events (player
possessions, pass outcomes, shots) 231, 24% and 15.

The specialist is trained on the 64 PFF FC World Cup 2022 matches in that reading (56 for training, 8 for early
stopping), each half in two simulated degradations. Per frame (25 fps) and per side it sees the ball's state and the
five nearest players of each team, relative to the ball and rotated to the side's attacking direction; a shared frame
encoder and a bidirectional GRU (±2 s around 2 s cores, symmetric over the two sides) output P(home control),
P(away control), P(dead), per-team "gains control" / "loses control" heat maps and a separate per-team touch head, so
that touching the ball and gaining control are learnt apart. It never saw DFL, Metrica, SkillCorner or BAR-ATH, so it
scores all of them out of sample. It is used in three places:

- **Team probability:** p = 0.75 × the blend of section 3.3 + 0.25 × the specialist's P(home control) among live
  frames, before the ±1 s smoothing and the decoder. This is the largest part of its gain.
- **Verifier features:** over each candidate, the candidate team's mean and peak control, its gain peak at the start,
  its loss peak at the end, its control in the ±2 s around, its peak and mean touch, and the other team's peak touch at
  the end.
- **Insert candidates:** runs of ≥ 6 frames inside a decoded possession where the specialist's control of the other
  team exceeds 0.7 and both teams have a player within 3 m of the ball, unless the blend already proposes the same
  interval (the threshold is the smallest of 0.6 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 with at most 25 candidates per half, chosen without
  labels).

On BAR-ATH the specialist agrees with v14's team decision on 94.3% of v14's possession frames (external sets
91.4–95.5%). v15 differs from v14 on 0.92% of the frames, mostly sub-second boundary shifts (216 → 207 possessions).

Since v17 the specialist is **J1**: the same network fine-tuned on the ten open games in the same reading (DFL
event-derived controlled, the Metrica sample games; `models/kpu_j1/`), 2,000 steps at learning rate 3e-4, every batch
half their windows and half C1's own PFF windows. The Metrica sample ball sits on its owner (a player within 0.3 m of
it on 44% of the clean frames, against 6.5% on DFL), so those windows carry 0.8 m of extra ball noise, which puts the
ball as far from the players as an automatic tracker's. That check mattered: on such input half of C1's gain on the
Metrica games disappeared. Weight, threshold and verifier recipe are unchanged; the verifier is retrained on J1's
outputs (`models/short_verifier_{ins,del}_j1m25s.txt`). v17 differs from v16 on 0.43% of the frames (207 → 208
possessions).

In v20 the team probability is p = 0.5 × the blend of section 3.3 + 0.5 × J1's P(home control). Until then only J1 had been scored on Metrica's
de-glued ball; v10 and the BiGRU still saw the glued one, which flattered Metrica by 0.006 (0.855 to 0.849). With the ball de-glued for every channel the weight 0.5,
pre-registered with 0.15 and 0.25, gains +0.006 on the primary contexts (90% interval [+0.001, +0.009]), with no guard context losing; 0.35 to 0.65 is a plateau, J1 alone loses.
Retraining v10 on the de-glued Metrica rows adds nothing. The earlier choice of 0.25 (round 27) had been made with the glued ball. On SoccerTrack v2 the step gains +0.011.

### 3.7 Fused dead-ball evidence (v18, v19, v20)

Until v17 the rules of section 3.2 alone decided which stretches are dead, and a learned model only adjusted the boundaries.
That choice rested on a weak comparison: the external sets have no broadcast, so their "rules" understated what BAR-ATH has.
SkillCorner has a real flag for "the view shows the pitch" that behaves like BAR-ATH's broadcast validity (valid on 94% of
live and 28% of dead frames). Its process was transplanted onto DFL and Metrica: for every true live or dead segment of a half,
a SkillCorner segment of the same state and nearly the same length gives its flag, stretched in time (`src/exp_deadmix.py`;
it is only used to score rules that follow BAR-ATH's formula, never to train anything). In that condition the rules are the
weaker channel: frame F1 of dead 0.91 / 0.91 / 0.89 on DFL / Metrica / SkillCorner, against 0.98 / 0.96 / 0.89 for a LightGBM
dead-ball model trained on the 7 DFL matches (their own ball status, the same simulated degradation, tracking features
only; `models/dead_base_v3.txt`).

v18 adds half of that model's alive log-odds to the rules' before decoding. The weight was set weeks earlier on SkillCorner and
not tuned again. Bounding the learned log-odds, stronger view weights, a bias towards alive, other dead-ball penalties and minimum
durations all add nothing (within +-0.002 or negative): the plain sum sits on a broad optimum. v16's step that moved
boundaries onto the learned model's own decode adds less than 0.005 on top and is dropped. The metric explains part of the
gain: a false dead stretch splits or deletes a possession, a false live stretch only stretches one. The fusion can only lose
if the rules are much better on BAR-ATH (frame F1 about 0.97 or more) and the learned model much worse than anything measured.

On BAR-ATH the dead share falls from 0.497 to 0.451. Of the decode's frames, 5.9% go from dead to live: earlier restarts (43
stretches, 1.2% of the frames), later stops (75, 2.2%), rule-dead stretches removed altogether (19, 2.0%) and splits (8, 0.5%);
1.3% go the other way, mostly earlier stops and later restarts. Each group lies in the external sets' range (for instance 22
removed stretches per match on SkillCorner, 91% of those frames truly live).

The official rules say the public window is not a tuning set, so v19 removes everything the window shaped. Refitting the rules' form
on the open sets alone (thresholds by provider-balanced log-loss, weights by logistic regression, view weights on SkillCorner, whose flag
is real) lifts the rules by themselves far above the hand-set ones: DFL evctrl 0.682 to 0.752, Metrica 0.768 to 0.821, SkillCorner 0.642
to 0.691, PFF 0.535 to 0.538. The constants set while looking at the window did not generalise.

A dead model trained on three providers with equal total weight (the seven DFL matches, the three Metrica games with their ball de-glued,
the twenty SkillCorner matches; `models/dead_multi_v1.txt`) then beats the DFL-only model. On its own it has no safety net: slow noise on
its log-odds costs much more than on a fusion. So v19 takes 0.25 x the open-data rules + 0.75 x that model + the view terms, chosen before
the result by a written rule: at least 0.005 on the primary contexts, no guard below -0.01, no loss against v18 on PFF or SoccerTrack, and among
those the smallest worst-case regret under stress. The alternatives failed one of these: equal parts of rules and model lose 0.002 to 0.003 on
SoccerTrack, equal parts of rules, DFL model and multi-source model lose 0.001 on PFF. The decoder's settings stay: on the open sets other dead-ball
penalties and minimum durations move the primary contexts by at most 0.0023. Adding the 64 PFF matches to the model adds nothing.

On BAR-ATH v19 differs from v18 on 3.95% of the frames: 193 possessions (v18: 208), 105 dead-ball stretches (110), dead share 0.478 (0.451).

v20 rests on three further findings.

*The ball around stoppages.* `sim.V2` and `sim.V3` cut every dead-ball gap exactly at the true restart, so on the external sets the ball reappears on the restart frame at 55% (DFL) and
72% (Metrica) of the restarts; on raw PFF tracking, which has real gaps, at 3%. `sim.V6` redraws the ball around each stop and restart: visible, gone or mixed, with shares taken from
aggregate, label-free statistics of BAR-ATH's whole-match ball around the model's own boundaries (no public window, nothing tied to a frame; the same kind of calibration as V3). The
masks in live play stay V3's, except within 6 frames of a restart. v19 does not fall on V6 (DFL 0.794 to 0.796), so this artefact had not flattered it, but the dead-ball models are now
trained and judged there. With shares like raw PFF's (`sim.V6B`) the decision does not change.

*A sequence model.* A small convolution + bidirectional GRU at 5 Hz reads the same 59 tracking features, with auxiliary stop and restart heads and equal provider weight in every batch
(`src/exp_tdead.py`, seven folds, three seeds, `models/tdead_v1/`). With half of the learned weight on it, the primary contexts gain +0.012.

*Unseen domains.* On the two sets no model saw, that sequence model erred in opposite directions: on PFF, whose dead frames show high tempo, -0.013; on SoccerTrack v2, a slower game, +0.068, with
v19 calling too much dead (0.387 against a true 0.303). Scaling each input feature by the half's own median and interquartile range, without labels, removes a match's level: the primary contexts hold
(+0.010 against v19) and both independent sets gain (PFF +0.014, SoccerTrack +0.089). A further test holds a whole provider out of every dead-ball model, the condition BAR-ATH is in. The mix of the
LightGBM and the normalised sequence model is the only arm positive everywhere: DFL +0.011, tracking-derived +0.009, Metrica +0.006, SkillCorner +0.006 to +0.007. The sequence model alone breaks
when SkillCorner is held out (-0.020 to -0.026), a normalised LightGBM when DFL is (-0.025), and adding PFF as a fourth provider gains on PFF but gives most of the gain on SoccerTrack back (+0.035).

So v20's alive log-odds are 0.25 x the rules + 0.375 x the LightGBM + 0.375 x the normalised sequence model + the view terms, all refitted on V6. The decoder's settings stay: with the sequence model before normalisation, other
team and dead-ball penalties and minimum durations move the primary contexts by at most 0.002, and its stop and restart heads as time-varying costs add +0.002, so they are not used. Under the
stress test (slow noise on a learned channel, rules better or worse than measured) the largest regret falls from 0.092 to 0.009.

On BAR-ATH v20 differs from v19 on 3.97% of the frames (2.97% dead to live, 0.52% live to dead, 0.49% change of team): 192 possessions (v19: 193), 105 dead-ball stretches (105), dead share 0.454 (0.478).

## 4. Possession rules implemented

- A possession is a maximal run of one team with the ball alive. Dead ball is always D, never a possession.
- A change of possession needs controlled possession by the other team. This is encoded in the training labels
  (section 3.3), in the decoder's switch penalty and soft minimum length, and in the controlled-possession reading
  that labels the specialist's and the verifier's training data (sections 3.5, 3.6).
- During loose or contested phases the decoder keeps the previous team unless the evidence for the other team
  persists.
- After a stoppage the possession is re-decided from the evidence of the first seconds of play (restart formation,
  who is on the ball).

## 5. Missing and noisy tracking

- The ball is missing on 41% of graded frames, mostly while it is dead. In play the gaps are short once filled from
  the broadcast ball. Missing values stay NaN; the gradient-boosted trees handle them natively, and the ball-free team
  features keep the classifier informed when the ball is lost.
- No player identities and slot swaps: every feature is collective (team level), never per slot.
- Noise in positions and in the ball: the classifier is trained on open tracking degraded the same way (section 3.3),
  and ±1 s logit smoothing plus the decoder's duration prior suppress flicker.
- The ATD fills some short ball gaps by prediction (over-smooth straight runs). Removing them was tested and not
  supported on external data, so they are kept.

## 6. Validation and model selection

Every idea was measured on held-out external matches with a fixed protocol:

- **DFL** leave-one-match-out (7 matches), labelled with a tracking-derived controlled-possession reading.
- **Metrica** leave-one-game-out (3 games × 3 degradations), controlled-possession labels from events.
- **SkillCorner** 20 A-League matches (broadcast tracking, never used for training), with two label conventions:
  phases of play and player possessions.

Each set is scored with the model's own dead-ball estimate and with the true dead ball. DFL is also scored with
controlled possession derived from its synchronised event data, which gives 10 contexts.
Decisions use the worst-case regret over the contexts. A difference below 0.005 keeps the simpler or current model.
From round 24 on, the rule was fixed before the results: the primary contexts are those that follow the challenge's
controlled-possession definition (Metrica, DFL event-derived; own and true dead ball), whose worst-case regret must
fall by ≥ 0.005, and no other context (DFL tracking-derived, SkillCorner phases / player possessions) may lose more
than 0.01. Every variant of the specialist was written down before it was run.
Candidates are checked on at least 3 LightGBM seeds and with a paired match bootstrap. Stress tests use unseen
degradations (pre-smoothed tracking, ATD-like predicted ball runs).

The verifier (section 3.5) was judged in the same way: every match is scored by a verifier that never saw it
(leave-one-match-out over 30 matches, the three sources pooled), over three team-model seeds, both dead-ball channels
and two verifier seeds, with neighbouring thresholds as a check.

The BiGRU blend needed one more step. The shipped BiGRU checkpoints were trained on all seven DFL matches, so DFL
could not judge anything that uses them. The BiGRU was therefore retrained seven times with the same recipe, each time
without one DFL match (three seeds each, on a cloud GPU), and DFL is scored with these held-out probabilities, both in
the blend and in the verifier's margin. Each blend seed is paired with one team-model seed. With the held-out
probabilities two things came to light: the GRU alone is weaker than the classifier on DFL (frame accuracy 0.90–0.91
against 0.91), so the 0.75 weight chosen earlier without DFL lost there; and the previous submission (v13 = the
classifier + the verifier, trained with DFL rows lacking a BiGRU margin) scores 0.006–0.012 lower on DFL once its
verifier sees a held-out margin, as it does on BAR-ATH. The submission was chosen among the pre-registered weights,
with and without the verifier, against v13 scored that way.

In November three more conditions of this protocol were corrected, each after a check of how the external sets differ from BAR-ATH: the Metrica ball for every team channel
(section 3.6), the ball mask around stoppages, and the hold-out level for dead-ball models, which now also leaves a whole provider out (section 3.7). The 64 raw PFF matches and SoccerTrack v2 stay
independent tests. PFF's dead ball is reconstructed from its events (out-of-play event to the next controlled action) and SoccerTrack's and DFL's are the providers' own per-frame status.

The 5-minute public window (17 possessions) is used only to check that the pipeline is correct; its bootstrap
interval (0.44–0.83 spellF1) is far too wide to rank versions. One exception from the first day is stated openly: the
dead-ball rules up to v18 were developed while checking them against that window, and two learned alternatives were rejected by
looking at it. An audit against the official rules, which call the window "not a tuning set", found this still in the code, so v19 replaces
every one of those constants with values derived from open data, and v18 and v19 were decided on the external sets without looking at
the window. One trace remains: tactical ball gaps are filled from the broadcast only where the two cameras agree within 2.5 m and at least four players
are visible. That gate dates from the same day and cannot be checked on the external sets, none of which has a second camera. v19 and v20 were decided without reading their scores on the window.

Team model and decoder (the v10 recipe, before the blend and the verifier):

| Set | v10 recipe, LightGBM seed 0 (as in the submission) | Mean of 3 LightGBM seeds | Earlier version (v7) |
|---|---|---|---|
| DFL (7 matches) | 0.773 / 0.801 | 0.769 / 0.798 | 0.760 / 0.782 |
| Metrica (3 games) | 0.824 / 0.882 | 0.823 / 0.882 | 0.815 / 0.872 |
| SkillCorner, phases (20 matches) | 0.598 / 0.759 | 0.597 / 0.759 | 0.582 / 0.746 |

## 8. What did not work (selected)

Each of these is ≤ +0.003 or negative on the external protocol:

- decoder variants beyond the soft minimum length (restart-aware, time-varying switch costs, insertion and deletion
  scorers);
- sequence models on their own (a bidirectional GRU, temporal stacking); blended with the classifier, the shared
  BiGRU does help (section 3.3), but a 0.75 weight loses on DFL;
- a player-level controller model;
- role features;
- duel-outcome features and a contest specialist;
- ball-touch event features;
- adding the broadcast-tracked SkillCorner matches to training;
- self-training on the test match;
- ensembles;
- ball height (even the true height from the open data);
- moving decoded possession changes to the optimum of less-smoothed evidence (the lag of short possessions comes from
  the team model's feature windows as well as from the decoder);
- the rule "the restarting team did not touch the ball last" to recover possessions before a stoppage (it tells the
  last touch, not the last control);
- broadcast camera framing as possession evidence;
- player names in the commentary;
- weights of the team channels that depend on the ball's visibility or the specialist's own change heads, directional switch costs from those heads, separate smoothing per channel;
- a richer view channel, team-side features in the dead-ball classifier, a normalised LightGBM, and PFF as a fourth dead-ball provider (section 3.7).

## 9. Limitations

- The remaining errors are short (< 4 s) in-play possessions after turnovers, especially duels and aerial balls, and
  their mirror image, spurious changes. Around those moments the tracking positions carry little more information
  than the model already uses; a simulation with perfect positions gains only about +0.005. The verifier recovers
  part of them, but its insertions are only weakly separable on DFL and Metrica (AUC about 0.7, with or without the
  BiGRU margin). What is missing is which team's player actually touched or controlled the ball, which would need
  reliable touch recognition from video.
- The BiGRU's weight is a compromise between the sets: on DFL, where the classifier is trained on the same kind of
  data, the GRU adds little; on SkillCorner, which neither model trained on, the blend gains most.
- Possession conventions differ between the training sets and the ground truth's provider, which is why model
  selection uses several conventions.
- The dead-ball evidence uses the broadcast recording's view; without it the model would rely on the tracking evidence only.
- The view flag on DFL and Metrica is transplanted from SkillCorner, a simulation, and the broadcast-ball gate of section 6 cannot be
  checked on the external sets.
- The ball masks of the external sets are simulated. `sim.V6`'s shares come from BAR-ATH's aggregates around the model's own boundaries, not the true ones, so the real alignment lies somewhere between V3 and V6. Both V6 and V6B
  give the same decision, and raw PFF is the only external set with real gaps.
- On SoccerTrack v2, a set no model saw, the dead ball remains the larger loss (0.794 against 0.85 with the true dead ball). BAR-ATH is also unseen, so this may hold there too.
- The verifier has not been retrained on v20's base, so a small gain may remain there.
- The ground truth's rule is unpublished. Frame-level labels, frame alignment and the timing of changes behave on the public window as our reading expects, but the window holds more short in-play possessions between two possessions of
  the other team than our controlled reading (0.99 per live minute against 0.20–0.24), and the model finds 10 possessions of 17 there. The evidence is thin (five minutes, four such possessions) and nothing was tuned on it, but the scores in section 7 may be optimistic: under looser
  readings of the open sets v20 scores 0.69–0.71.

## 10. Reproducing the submission

```bash
# Python 3.12; pinned packages in requirements.txt
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/Scripts/python.exe -r requirements.txt
git clone https://github.com/metrica-sports/more-than-a-hack-2027 external/more-than-a-hack-2027
# match bundle -> data/{tactical,broadcast} (or set MTAH_DATA_DIR)
python src/make_submission.py               # -> submissions/candidate_v20.csv
python external/more-than-a-hack-2027/evaluation/validate_submission.py submissions/candidate_v20.csv

# optional: retrain the team classifier from the open data (rewrites models/v10_team.txt)
python src/download_idsse.py                # open DFL / IDSSE data, CC BY 4.0, ~2.6 GB
python src/metrica_sample.py download       # Metrica sample games, pinned commit, ~185 MB
MTAH_RETRAIN=1 python src/make_submission.py
```

- **Default run.** The team classifier is shipped as `models/v10_team.txt` (2.9 MB, trained only on the open data),
  the specialist as `models/kpu_j1/kpu_J1_s20261102.pt` (0.9 MB, open data only), the dead-ball models as
  `models/dead_multi_v2.txt` and `models/tdead_v1/` (three checkpoints, 2.5 MB each), the rule weights as `models/dead_rules_open_v2.json` (open data only), and the shared BiGRU as
  `models/bigru_dfl_pff_v1/`. The default run therefore needs only the provided data and the official repository (for
  the scorer and the public window). On the first run it also rebuilds the BiGRU's BAR-ATH probabilities on the CPU
  (`src/reproduce_shared_bigru.py`, a few minutes; it checks the result against the checkpoints' manifest) and runs
  the specialist and the sequence model on the CPU. `--model model_v19`, `--model model_v18`, `--model model_v17`, `--model model_v16`, `--model model_v15`, `--model model_v14` and `--model model_v13` still write the previous
  submissions.
- **Retraining.** `MTAH_RETRAIN=1` rebuilds the simulated training inputs, the features and the team classifier from
  the open data in about 7 minutes on 24 cores; the submission is unchanged. The verifier classifiers come from the
  research pipeline (`src/exp_verify.py`, held-out team-model and BiGRU probabilities on the external sets; on DFL the
  leave-one-match-out BiGRU of `src/exp_bigru_lomo.py`, trained on a GPU with the PFF data; for v15 also the
  specialist's outputs on the external sets, `src/exp_kpu.py`) and are retrained byte for byte with
  `MTAH_RETRAIN_VERIFIER=1` when those caches exist. The specialist was trained on a cloud GPU from the PFF data
  (`src/short_specialist.py prep-pff` / `train`) and fine-tuned on the local GPU (`finetune`).
  `MTAH_RETRAIN_DEAD=1` retrains v19's dead-ball models from the open data, and `python src/dead_rules_fit.py` re-derives the rule
  constants; the retrain of the older DFL model is not byte-identical to its shipped file (written on 21 October), so
  `MTAH_RETRAIN=1` leaves them alone. v20's: `python src/dead_v6_fit.py rules`, `python src/dead_v6_fit.py multi`, and for the sequence model, on a GPU in about 10 minutes per seed,
  `TD_V6=1 TD_NORM=1 TD_OUT=tdead6n python src/exp_tdead.py train <seed>` followed by `python src/dead_v6_fit.py td`.
- **Checks on Windows, Python 3.12.13, from an empty cache:**
  - the retrained model file is byte-identical to the shipped one;
  - both runs write the same submission (MD5 above).
- **Determinism.** Simulation seeds are fixed, LightGBM runs in deterministic mode with a fixed seed and thread count,
  and no GPU is used. LightGBM's deterministic mode is guaranteed for a fixed platform and thread count; on another
  platform a retrain could differ in the last bits, which is one more reason the trained classifier is shipped.
- **Line endings.** LightGBM 4.7 cannot read a model file with CRLF line endings, which a Windows checkout with Git's
  default `core.autocrlf=true` writes for text files. `.gitattributes` keeps `models/*.txt` byte for byte, and the
  pipeline reads the models as text (`src/bench.py`, `load_booster`), so a converted copy loads the same model.
- All intermediate files go to `cache/` (gitignored).

## 11. Data, licences and policy

- No match data and nothing derived from it at frame level is in the repository. `data/`, `cache/` and
  `submissions/` are gitignored.
- Open data is downloaded from its sources and not redistributed:
  - IDSSE / DFL (CC BY 4.0, Bassek et al. 2025, figshare 28196177);
  - Metrica Sports sample data (credited as requested by its README);
  - SkillCorner open data (MIT);
  - PFF FC / Gradient Sports FIFA World Cup 2022 data, obtained through the provider's access form and used by a team
    member to train the shared BiGRU checkpoints (the checkpoints contain no match data), by us to train the
    leave-one-DFL-match-out copies used for validation and for the verifier's DFL margins (not shipped), and to train
    the short-possession specialist (shipped; tracking and human-labelled events only);
  - SoccerTrack v2, used as an independent test only.
- The simulator's rates (`sim.V3`, `sim.V6`) use aggregate, label-free statistics of the provided tracking over the whole match; no model is trained on the provided match.
- The labels are produced entirely by the algorithm; no frame was annotated by hand.
